summary.text: Water vapor is water in its gas form, produced when liquid water evaporates or boils or when ice sublimes.
It is transparent and less dense than most other gases in air, so it triggers convection currents that can lead to clouds and fog.
In Earth's atmosphere it acts as a greenhouse gas, contributing more to the total greenhouse effect than carbon dioxide or methane.

facts.label: US pan evaporation
facts.value: From under 30 to over 120 inches a year

facts.label: Most vapor in air
facts.value: About 30 g per m³, saturated at 30 °C

facts.label: Found beyond Earth
facts.value: The Sun's atmosphere and every Solar System planet

items.prompt: You climb out of a pool on a breezy day and feel suddenly chilly. Why?

options.label: The pool water was colder than the air
Evaporating water carries off your heat
Moving air is always colder than still air
Wet skin blocks the warmth of the Sun

items.explain: Liquid water that turns to vapor takes heat with it, a process called evaporative cooling.

items.prompt: Water vapor condenses into dew on a cold car windscreen. What does that do to the glass surface?

options.label: It cools the glass down even more
It has no effect on its temperature
It freezes the glass right away
It warms the glass slightly

items.explain: When vapor condenses onto a surface, each water molecule brings heat energy with it, so the surface warms.

items.prompt: In midwinter, snow slowly disappears even though it is far too cold to melt. Where does it go?

options.label: It turns straight into vapor
It sinks into the frozen soil
It is packed down into ice
It is eaten by soil bacteria

items.explain: Through sublimation, water molecules leave ice directly without becoming liquid, slowly removing snow at temperatures too low to melt it.

items.prompt: Over thousands of years, wide areas of Antarctic snow have turned to vapor and vanished. What valuable things does this leave exposed?

options.label: Buried oil and gas deposits
Ancient frozen animal remains
Well-preserved meteorites
Fresh liquid water lakes

items.explain: Sublimed snow leaves behind its non-volatile contents, including meteorites exposed in large numbers and excellent condition.

items.prompt: Why do scientists describe water vapor as a feedback in warming?

options.label: It only appears once warming has ended
It amplifies warming that something else began
It cools the planet once it condenses
It is released mainly by power plants

items.explain: Water vapor responds to temperature changes and amplifies the effect of whatever first caused the warming.

items.prompt: A glass of iced drink gets beads of water on the outside. When does water vapor condense onto a surface like this?

options.label: When the surface is cooler than the dew point
Whenever the air feels warm and a bit sticky
Only when rain is falling outside at the time
When liquid seeps through the glass walls

items.explain: Vapor condenses onto a surface only when that surface is cooler than the dew point, or when the air's vapor equilibrium is exceeded.

paragraphs.heading: Water as a gas
paragraphs.text: Water vapor is water in its gas form. It forms when liquid water evaporates or boils, or when ice sublimes, which means its molecules leave the ice directly without first becoming liquid. Like most gases in the air, it is transparent. In ordinary conditions it is constantly made by evaporation and removed by condensation.

paragraphs.heading: A powerful greenhouse gas
paragraphs.text: Water vapor is less dense than most other gases in air, and it sets off convection currents that can build clouds and fog. In Earth's atmosphere it acts as a greenhouse gas, adding more to the overall greenhouse effect than carbon dioxide or methane do. It is called a feedback because it responds to temperature changes and amplifies whatever started the warming. It also turns up far beyond Earth: in the Sun's atmosphere, on every planet in the Solar System, and on moons, comets and even large asteroids.

paragraphs.heading: Evaporation cools
paragraphs.text: A water molecule that leaves a surface and spreads into the gas around it is said to have evaporated. Water that turns into vapor carries some heat away with it, a process called evaporative cooling. How much vapor is already in the air decides how often molecules return to the surface. When evaporation wins overall, the remaining water cools in step with the water lost. Evaporative cooling is limited by conditions in the atmosphere.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring the vapor
paragraphs.text: The water vapor content of air, called humidity, is measured with instruments called hygrometers. Readings are usually given as specific humidity or as percent relative humidity. Humidity ranges from 0 grams per cubic metre in dry air to 30 grams per cubic metre when the vapor is saturated at 30 °C. In the US, the National Weather Service measures evaporation from standard open pans of water outdoors, and yearly totals run from under 30 to over 120 inches.

paragraphs.heading: Snow that vanishes
paragraphs.text: Sublimation explains the slow midwinter disappearance of ice and snow at temperatures too low for melting. Antarctica shows this strongly, as it is by far the continent with the least precipitation on Earth. Across large areas there, snow layers built up over millennia have sublimed away, leaving behind the material that does not evaporate. This has exposed meteorites in unmatched numbers and in excellent condition, which is very valuable to some sciences.

paragraphs.heading: Condensation warms
paragraphs.text: Water vapor condenses onto a surface only when that surface is colder than the dew point, or when the vapor balance in the air has been exceeded. When it does, the surface warms, because each water molecule brings heat energy with it. In turn, the air cools slightly. In the atmosphere, condensation makes clouds, fog and precipitation, usually only when cloud condensation nuclei help it along.
